More than half of the nodes; the smallest group allowed to make a decision.

before.note: Read CAP and Replication first: consensus is how replicas stay in agreement so a system can be strongly consistent while a quorum survives. The terms below are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: Consensus is the problem of getting a group of machines to agree on a single value, or a single order of values, even when some crash and messages are lost or delayed. It is the foundation under strongly consistent stores. etcd, a consistent key-value store that Kubernetes uses as its backing store [[kube-etcd]], replicates all its data within a single consistent replication group, so a modification only needs to go through the Raft protocol to commit [[etcd-why]].

The classic academic solution is Paxos, which the Raft authors call quite difficult to understand, in spite of numerous attempts to make it more approachable [[raft-paper]]. Raft was designed to be easy to understand and is equivalent to Paxos in fault-tolerance and performance; its authors hope it will make consensus available to a wider audience [[raft]]. Because Raft is understandable and etcd commits through it, it is a good one to learn first.

The heart of every such protocol is the majority. The Raft page says typical consensus algorithms make progress when any majority of their servers is available: a cluster of 5 servers can keep operating with 2 failed, and if more fail they stop making progress but never return an incorrect result [[raft]]. Because any two majorities share at least one node, the group cannot agree to two conflicting decisions; that single idea lets the system keep going while a minority is down and stop rather than disagree when it cannot reach a majority.

terms.definition: Agreeing on one value or order across replicas despite crashes and lost messages.
The original consensus algorithm: correct but notoriously hard to understand.
A consensus algorithm designed for understandability, equivalent in power to Paxos.
The set of replicas that run consensus together to agree on one log of changes.

stages.name: How it works
body: Raft runs with one leader and several followers, all holding an identical append-only log. Clients send commands to the leader; the leader appends each to its log and replicates it to the followers so every log is the same sequence in the same order [[raft-paper]]. This single-leader, single-log shape is what makes the protocol easy to reason about.

Time is divided into terms, each with at most one leader. A follower that stops hearing the leader's heartbeats times out, becomes a candidate, and asks the others for votes; a candidate that collects a majority becomes the leader for a new term. A node only grants its vote to a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own, which means a new leader holds every committed entry [[raft-paper]].

An entry becomes committed once the leader that created it has replicated it on a majority of the servers, after which it is applied and acknowledged [[raft-paper]]. etcd states the practical consequence: because it has a single replication group, a modification only needs to go through the Raft protocol to commit [[etcd-why]].

terms.definition: The ordered, append-only list of commands every replica keeps identical.
A span of time with at most one leader; a new election begins a new term.
A timed-out follower becomes a candidate and wins a majority of votes to lead.
An entry is committed once a majority has stored it, then applied in order everywhere.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: The subtle part of consensus is reads, not writes. A leader that was just deposed during a partition might still think it leads and serve stale data. The Raft paper says a leader must check whether it has been deposed by exchanging heartbeats with a majority before answering a read-only request [[raft-paper]]. etcd's guide describes the same cost: linearizable reads go through a quorum of members to fetch the most recent data, while serializable reads are cheaper because a single member serves them, in exchange for possibly stale data [[etcd-perf]].

The common optimisation is a lease on leadership, so the leader can answer reads from local state without checking a majority each time. The Raft paper mentions the idea, and warns that relying on heartbeats as a lease depends on timing for safety, because it assumes bounded clock skew [[raft-paper]]. The topic's CockroachDB post shows leases taken to scale, folding the lease into Raft leadership to cut its overhead.

Sizing follows from the majority rule. A cluster of five can tolerate the failure of any two servers [[raft-paper]], and the Kubernetes docs say to run etcd with an odd number of members and recommend five in production [[kube-etcd]]. General reasoning, not from the cited pages: an even number buys nothing extra, since four nodes tolerate the same single failure as three but need a larger majority to agree. So consensus clusters are usually three or five nodes, chosen for the failure budget you need, not for raw capacity.

terms.definition: A read guaranteed to see the latest committed write, which naively needs a majority round trip.
A bounded grant of leadership that lets the leader serve reads locally without checking a majority.
Kubernetes' etcd guide says to run an odd number of members; the Raft page's example is a five-server cluster that survives two failures.
Two nodes both acting as leader; the etcd page says the systems it targets will never tolerate this and will sacrifice availability to avoid it.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: The headline trade-off is latency for agreement. etcd's performance guide is explicit that consensus commit latency is limited by two physical costs: network round-trip time between members and the disk sync on each member, with a typical US round trip around 50 ms and up to 400 ms between continents, and a disk sync around 10 ms on a spinning disk versus under 1 ms on an SSD [[etcd-perf]]. The guide says etcd raises throughput by batching requests. Our reading of its figures: SSDs and nearby members would shrink the two costs, but nothing removes the round trip.

Placement is the other practical lever. Because every commit needs a majority, a cluster whose majority is spread across continents pays a cross-region round trip on every write; that is general reasoning from the round-trip figures above, not something the etcd page spells out. The etcd page does note that systems which partition data across multiple consistent replication groups (shards) are the ones used for large data sets, while etcd keeps one group for a few GB [[etcd-why]].

Finally, consensus is where availability meets correctness from CAP. As long as a majority of the cluster is reachable, the system keeps making progress, and when too many servers fail it stops making progress but never returns an incorrect result [[raft]]. etcd's page says the systems it is built for will never tolerate split-brain operation and are willing to sacrifice availability to achieve this [[etcd-why]].

terms.definition: The time to agree and durably store a write, bounded by network and disk.
Grouping many requests into one consensus round to raise throughput.
One set of replicas that run consensus together; etcd keeps all its data in a single group.
Losing a majority, after which the cluster blocks rather than risk disagreement.

misconceptions.myth: A two-node cluster is a cheap way to get fault tolerance.
misconceptions.truth: A majority of two is two, so losing either node stops progress. The Raft page's example is five servers that keep operating with two failed [[raft]], and Kubernetes advises an odd number of members [[kube-etcd]].

misconceptions.myth: The leader can always answer reads from its own memory for free.
misconceptions.truth: The Raft paper says a leader must first check with a majority that it has not been deposed, unless it relies on a heartbeat lease that assumes bounded clock skew [[raft-paper]].

misconceptions.myth: Consensus is slow because the code is unoptimised.
misconceptions.truth: etcd's guide says the minimum time for a request is the network round trip between members plus the time fdatasync needs to commit to disk [[etcd-perf]].

misconceptions.myth: Paxos and Raft give different guarantees.
misconceptions.truth: The Raft page says Raft is equivalent to Paxos in fault-tolerance and performance; it is organised to be easier to understand [[raft]].

tryIt.intro: These use etcdctl against a local or test etcd cluster to see its members, its leader and a committed write. They are the commands on the etcd pages cited below. Output depends on your cluster, so it is not shown here. Replace $ENDPOINTS with your endpoints.

commands.shows: The members of the cluster, so you can see how many there are.
The status of each endpoint as a table; the page's example output includes an IS LEADER column.
Writes the key foo with the value bar. In a Raft cluster the write is committed once it has been replicated on a majority of members.
commands.warning: This writes a key to the cluster. Run only against a test cluster.
